title_en: El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations
excerpt_en: Haiti’s war on gangs is increasingly relying on a patchwork of foreign troops and private militias, making accountability more complicated.
body_en: A Salvadoran Army soldier stands guard at a camp in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct. 31, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images On Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele posted footage of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

He had earlier requested, via a social media post in Haitian Creole, the address of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal organizations. Bukele subsequently claimed the operation, conducted with Haitian police, had demolished Joseph’s residence and gang headquarters. As many as 20 people were killed, although Joseph was reportedly absent.

The attack comes amid a flurry of anti-gang operations in Haiti. On Nov. 6, Mathias Saintil, head of the “Boston” gang in Cité Soleil, was killed in a drone strike by a Haitian special task force, prompting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé to declare on the social media platform X “one less gang leader.” Erik Prince, founder of the private military firm Vectus Global, responded: “Nice shot.”

As an expert on organized crime in Latin America and the Caribbean, I believe these operations mark both a dramatic escalation in Haiti’s fight against organized crime and the first overseas test of Bukele’s security model. The intervention is drawing support from some regional leaders and pro-Bukele networks, even as concerns grow over civilian casualties and whether military gains can translate into lasting security.

Rescue mission or military offensive? El Salvador already had a limited presence in Haiti as one of six countries contributing personnel to the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, or GSF. The force was authorized in 2025 to help Haitian authorities reclaim cities and streets from violent gangs that control swathes of the impoverished nation. But it remains severely understaffed and has struggled to translate military operations into lasting territorial gains.
Then, in an Oct. 18 gang ambush, four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the Gang Suppression Force disappeared. Their burned vehicle was recovered, but their fate remains uncertain.

Either way, Bukele used the incident to justify expanding El Salvador’s military presence in Haiti. Within weeks he had sent roughly 2,500 troops, along with armored vehicles and attack helicopters, in what he initially called a rescue mission.

They joined an already crowded battlefield. Haiti’s police and army operate alongside the GSF, authorized but not commanded by the United Nations. The Haitian task force involved in operations against Saintil also works with former Blackwater CEO Prince’s Vectus Global, while vigilante groups patrol contested neighborhoods. Dozens of armed gangs associated with the gang coalition Viv Ansanm control large parts of Port-au-Prince and operate beyond the capital.

Special forces from El Salvador ride in a Gang Suppression Force truck in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct 23, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images The Gang Suppression Force was authorized by the U.N. Security Council to deploy up to 5,550 personnel, and it currently has roughly 2,000 on the ground. Most of the Salvadoran troops now in Haiti operate outside its command. Haitian Prime Minister Fils-Aimé insists that Haiti directs the operations. Yet neither government has publicly disclosed the agreement specifying Salvadoran authority, rules of engagement or the deployment’s duration.
Without a published deployment agreement, the chain of command and rules for authorizing strikes remain unclear to the public.

Despite President Donald Trump’s support for Bukele, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has distanced Washington from the Salvadoran offensive, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He warned that poor coordination could lead to friendly fire, while U.S. diplomats formally protested the risks to multinational troops and civilian personnel.

Salvadoran authorities dispute American allegations that their gunfire struck the U.S. embassy and endangered multinational troops. They also questioned the credibility of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti.
Uncertain rules of engagement Haiti’s security crisis is dire.

In recent years, organized violence has reached levels associated with armed conflict. Almost 6,000 people were killed in 2025, and more than 4,000 in the first nine months of 2026. Nearly 1.5 million Haitians have been displaced as of August 2026, and expanded offensives and gang reprisals could drive more from their homes.

An independent legal assessment by the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights classifies fighting between Haitian forces and the Viv Ansanm coalition as a noninternational armed conflict, a legal category that includes civil wars. The International Committee of the Red Cross has separately warned of the risks to civilians, urging all sides to respect international law.

The distinction matters because the rules on lethal force are different in war and policing. Both require civilians to be protected. But in an armed conflict, members of armed groups with combat roles can be targeted even when they pose no immediate threat. In a police operation, simply being suspected of gang membership is not enough to justify killing someone – lethal force is generally allowed only when necessary to protect lives.

Of particular concern is the growing use of explosive drones and helicopter attacks in residential areas. At least 1,243 people were killed in 141 drone operations between March 2025 and January 2026, including at least 60 people reportedly unconnected to gangs, 17 of them children. These operations predated the Salvadoran escalation but demonstrate the risks of using explosive weapons in populated areas.
At the same time, overlapping mandates for foreign troops and private military contractors could complicate investigations into civilian casualties and allegations of unlawful attacks.

title_en: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
excerpt_en: Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
body_en: The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.

Ecosystem at risk The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.

It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.
Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.

Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.

“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.

“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”

Strikes and spills Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.

Interactive “Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.

More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.

Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.

Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.

Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.

Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.

Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.

Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.

title_en: World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns
excerpt_en: Failure to cut emissions will ‘consign humanity to disasters they are unable to adapt to’, report says
body_en: The world is heading for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions, analysis has found.

Under current policies, the planet will heat up by 2.7C on average by the end of the century compared with preindustrial times, the report by Climate Action Tracker (CAT) found. This is up slightly from a prediction of 2.6C in the group’s analysis conducted last year.

This level of warming smashes the 1.5C threshold that was agreed by countries a decade ago but is set to be breached in just a few years. Scientists have warned that beyond this point already harmful storms, droughts, heatwaves, flooding and other impacts will become intolerable for parts of the world and potentially trigger runaway climate change that won’t be contained.
Related: ‘My classroom was 30C. No one was learning. Then I started to feel dizzy’ – This is climate breakdown

Countries, minus the US, are gathered in the Turkish city of Antalya for UN climate talks that have centred on the looming “overshoot” of the temperature target. This reality should compel governments to act quickly to phase out use of the fossil fuels that are causing the climate crisis, the UN secretarygeneral, António Guterres, said on Tuesday.

If countries did act decisively to slash emissions then the future temperature projections would become less daunting, the CAT report states. However, in even the most optimistic scenario – where all pledges, targets and other long-term promises made by countries were fulfilled – the world would still heat up by 1.9C by the end of the century.
Such targets have been routinely flouted by the countries that have made them, however. This means leaders face a crunch moment, experts say.

“The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to – or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever,” says Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics.

Hare said exceeding 1.5C warming “cannot be an excuse to open the door to defeatism” and that every small increment of temperature rise will be significant. The CAT analysis is similar to one recently put out by the UN, which uses previous CAT data to inform its own projections.
Related: National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns

While the world is failing to cut emissions in line with the science and countries’ own promises, carbon pollution is set to dip slightly this year and CAT pointed to some causes for optimism. Clean energy investment is now double that of fossil fuels, electric car use is soaring and the deforestation of the Amazon in Brazil has fallen sharply.

But much more will need to be done to avert disastrous climate impacts. Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate advocate, arrived in Antalya on Tuesday and warned that “everything and everyone we love is at stake” because of the failure to confront the climate crisis.

“Governments collectively are simply not moving fast enough to adopt the policies that would enable us to escape from the emerging overshoot trap,” said Sarah Heck, lead author of the CAT report. Some countries, such as the US, Canada and New Zealand, are even slowing down their climate action to a “staggering level”, she added.

title_en: Nvidia board reportedly meeting to decide CEO Jensen Huang’s future as chip giant’s share price plunges – follow live
excerpt_en: Huang’s potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4tn chipmaker he co-founded, with Nvidia’s shares sliding about 8% in after-hours trading
body_en: Donald Trump said on Monday he was “amazed” after the revelations concerning Jensen Huang – one of his ⁠closest allies in Silicon Valley – came to light. The president’s close ties with the Nvidia CEO have come under renewed scrutiny after revelations about the billionaire executive’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy were revealed.
Trump said on 9 November that Huang had told him he had no idea that the woman was a spy. The president added that he believed the CEO.
I asked him that question ’Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said ’I had no idea that she was a spy’ and I really believe him.”
I know the FBI is looking into it … I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Over the past two years, Huang has voiced support for the Trump administration’s AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market and ⁠lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to ⁠Nvidia’s sophisticated AI chips.
In May 2026, Huang was among a delegation of tech CEOs who joined Trump during his visit to China ‌to meet Xi Jinping, as the Republican leader urged Beijing to “open up” to US business.

Then in September, as the Trump administration and AI companies faced increasing scrutiny over risks posed by advanced AI, Trump announced that Huang was among a number of tech CEOs who had signed a voluntary safety pact and backed data center expansion.
Trump, who had argued previously that the US does not need new AI-specific regulations, said the pact was “morally binding,” prompting criticism that it was “toothless’” regulation.
In the previous week, Huang had attended a high-profile state dinner for Xi Jinping at the White House, accompanied by his wife.
In early October, Trump awarded the National Medal of Science, the United States’ highest honour for scientists and engineers, to the Nvidia CEO and some other tech industry leaders.

As recently as Tuesday, Nvidia was saying that Jensen Huang would continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”. That statement was made as the company announced it had appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.
The $4.1tn chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim.
Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors.

“The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not ‌a tail risk,” said Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder ‌of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares.
Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that Nvidia’s board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for Huang, citing a person familiar with the situation.

Rosenberg said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who has held the role for more than a decade, would be the natural choice as an interim CEO, but said the bigger question was who would lead Nvidia longer term.

How did we get here? Reports that Nvidia’s board is weighing Jensen Huang’s future at the company mark a dramatic escalation in events that began last week, when it was revealed that the CEO had been engaged in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.
The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government.

US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.

The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.
Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the US, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

title_en: Democrats are at Cop31 to show that the US has not abandoned the fight against climate change
excerpt_en: Democratic control of Congress means they have more power to challenge Trump’s environmental stance.
body_en: The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.
Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.

World leaders arrive at Cop31, but what will be the role of the unofficial US delegation? Data centres are big issue The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.
Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.

title_en: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
excerpt_en: The post A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A voter departs after casting a ballot at a polling location in Atlanta on Nov. 3. Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Image Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots.

The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters.
But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots.

The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices.

The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting.

In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious.

ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud.

Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.”

The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica.

How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica.
Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms.
“That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.”
Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally.

In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names.
Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone. The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead.

State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.”

Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name.

During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further.

But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.”
Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy.
“I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said.
The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter.

title_en: Australian states could sue tobacco companies for billions in healthcare costs under proposal
excerpt_en: Exclusive: Former barrister who helped legally establish that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer argues states could seek up to $50bn in compensation
body_en: Australian state governments could sue tobacco companies for billions in public hospital and healthcare costs, under a proposal developed by a former barrister who helped legally establish that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer.
The South Australian government is formally seeking advice on the proposal, while other states are reviewing it.

Authored by Sydney Health Law research affiliate Neil Francey, the proposal argues the states could file proceedings in the federal court seeking up to $50bn in compensation for health costs, and to fund cancer screening programs and prevention measures.
It targets the dominant tobacco companies in Australia – British American Tobacco (BAT), Philip Morris and Imperial Brands – and their parent corporations overseas.

Francey is presenting the blueprint at the Clinical Oncology Society of Australia’s annual scientific meeting in Sydney on Thursday, arguing the companies could be held liable for decades of misleading and deceptive conduct under Australian consumer law.
He has also briefed state government MPs. Under the plan, the six state governments would pool their resources to set up a dedicated, joint legal taskforce to run the case.
“For decades, the tobacco industry has unjustly enriched itself while distracting and confusing smokers about the harms and addictiveness of their product,” the proposal says.
Related: Illegal tobacco increasingly hard to spot, with some fakes in plain packaging featuring Australian health warnings

“The industry has not been forced to bear the full costs of the harm caused by their product. These costs have either been borne by smokers themselves, or by taxpayers when smokers get sick and receive publicly funded or subsidised health care.”

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email A BAT Australia spokesperson said the company does not comment on potential or pending legal claims, while Philip Morris and Imperial Brands did not respond to requests for comment.

Francey told Guardian Australia that the proposal excludes the Northern Territory and the ACT, as the territories are an arm of the commonwealth, and there are differences in healthcare funding arrangements that could complicate the case.

The proposal seeks to recover healthcare costs incurred by the states since 2000, when internal tobacco industry documents were published revealing the industry knew that smoking caused serious diseases but colluded to cover up and obfuscate the evidence.
“I think you can justify a figure in the order of fifty billion, possibly even more,” Francey said.

In 1991, Francey represented consumers in a federal court of Australia case triggered by a Tobacco Institute of Australia advertisement that claimed there was “nothing which proves scientifically that cigarette smoke causes disease in nonsmokers”.

The court found compelling scientific proof that passive smoking causes lung disease and respiratory conditions in non-smokers, making the industry’s claims unlawful. The historic ruling accelerated workplace and public indoor smoking bans.

Francey said his latest proposal has the benefit of being brought by state governments under consumer protection laws, bypassing some of the challenges faced by smokers pursuing personal injury lawsuits, where it can be hard to prove which brand caused the harm, and with tobacco companies arguing people have “ freedom of choice ”.
Francey said state governments could seek court orders against companies engaged in misleading and deceptive conduct which has led to loss and damage and the likelihood of suffering in future.

The South Australian health minister, Blair Boyer, said there was a “substantial” public interest in measures reducing the harms that tobacco-related diseases place on governments, health systems and communities.
“While this proposal draws on historic findings regarding misleading and deceptive conduct by the tobacco industry, it is important that the state does its own due diligence,” he said.
“I have sought advice on the proposal, the likelihood of success and the benefits to South Australians, which will allow the government to consider its options.”
A spokesperson for the NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said: “We will review his proposal carefully”.

A spokesperson for the Queensland health minister, Tim Nicholls, confirmed a meeting with Francey, but said the state was focused on laws targeting the illicit tobacco and vape trade. The Western Australian health minister, Meredith Hammat, said the state’s efforts are currently focused on strengthening tobacco legislation and enforcement activities.

title_en: Cabo Verde’s presidential election: the stakes in one of Africa’s most stable democracies
excerpt_en: The presidential election will test party loyalties and voters’ expectations of the presidency, as well as its role in the political system.
body_en: Cape Verde’s presidential election takes place against the backdrop of a democratic record that remains unusual in its regional context. The country, made up of an archipelago of islands off the coast of west Africa, has sustained multiparty competition for more than three decades. It has had peaceful transfers of power and no coups or military takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Cabo Verde (population 530,000) is a semi-presidential republic in which the president is directly elected. The prime minister is appointed by the president in light of parliamentary election results, and heads a government that is politically accountable to the national assembly.
The president represents the state and safeguards the constitution, while the prime minister and the government conduct public policy.

The presidency nevertheless carries substantial political weight. The president can veto legislation, request constitutional review and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. The office also entails responsibilities in foreign affairs and national defence.

The president is, therefore, not the principal policymaker. However, the way in which these powers are exercised can become particularly consequential when the president and prime minister belong to opposing political camps. This might indeed be the outcome of the 15 November 2026 election.

I am a political communication specialist who has researched the dynamics of Cabo Verde’s presidential elections. In my view the central test for the upcoming poll will be whether the country’s institutions can continue to function effectively while preserving the important distinction between the presidency and the government.

The background Cape Verde’s political climate is shaped by a recent change of government. The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde returned to office after winning the May 2026 parliamentary election. This ended 10 years of government by the Movement for Democracy, which now forms the opposition.

The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde’s victory reflected growing voter dissatisfaction with a decade of rule by the Movement for Democracy. This is particularly over poor inter-island transport, economic difficulties, living conditions and public security.

The change of government renewed questions about the balance of power between the president, the new government and parliament, as well as the opposition’s ability to hold the ruling party accountable.
The forthcoming presidential election will, therefore, test not only party loyalties but also voters’ expectations of the presidency and its role in the political system.
The two main contenders are José Maria Neves, backed by the African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde, and Joana Rosa, supported by the Movement for Democracy.
Neves previously served as prime minister between 2001 and 2016. Rosa, a former minister of justice, is the first woman to run for president in Cabo Verde.

They face Antero Tavares, Casimiro de Pina, Gilson Alves and Loisito Sousa. These four offer alternatives to the two parties that have dominated national politics since the introduction of multipartyism in 1991.
These candidates are unlikely, however, to attract support on a scale that would challenge the two main contenders.

The voters Together with political science researchers Danielton Delgado and Susana Rogeiro Nina, I published a paper that offers insight into the dynamics of presidential elections in Cabo Verde. Our 2019 study found that voters didn’t consistently use presidential contests to punish the governing party. Indeed, except in 2011 and 2021, every presidential election in the country was won by the candidate backed by the party that controlled parliament and the executive.

Also, there was not a systematic advantage for independent candidates or candidates backed by smaller parties. The short interval – one to six months – between legislative and presidential elections may help explain this phenomenon, as presidential contests often take place during the governing party’s post-election “honeymoon period”.

What’s different in the upcoming election? If Neves secures re-election, the presidency and government will be held by figures associated with the same party. This possibility is not unlikely. Since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991, every incumbent president who has sought a second term has been re-elected: António Mascarenhas Monteiro in 1996, Pedro Pires in 2006 and Jorge Carlos Fonseca in 2016.
A victory for Neves could play out in one of two ways. It could facilitate cooperation, but it could also raise questions about the president’s independence from the government.

In turn, a victory for Rosa, mirroring the patterns that emerged in 2011 and 2021, would create a situation of divided leadership, with a Movement for Democracy-backed president working alongside an African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde government.
Such an arrangement is not inherently problematic. Nevertheless, it can require negotiation when constitutional responsibilities and political interests diverge.

Cabo Verde has recent experience of this situation: between November 2021 and the formation of the new government in June 2026, Neves dealt with a Movement for Democracy government. This was led by Ulisses Correia e Silva. Despite their partisan differences, relations were generally characterised by institutional cooperation rather than open confrontation.

In short, whoever wins will face a distinct institutional challenge. Neves will have to balance his party affiliation with the constitutional responsibility to act as head of state. Rosa will need to establish a working relationship with a government led by her political opponents.

title_en: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
excerpt_en: The post A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Evelyn at the grave of her twin, Ginnifer The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms.

Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon.

Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him.

Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.)

No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born.
Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma.

The living room in the house where Ginnifer was born and died. Dozens of Followers of Christ members filled the home that day, but none called 911. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office Followers anoint the ailing with olive oil. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin?
There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive.
In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper.

He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

Evelyn, at 14 days old, was still so small she could fit into dolls’ clothes. Courtesy of the Phillips family Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death.
The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn?

Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn.

Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him.

Jennifer and Marshall Phillips For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves.
Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question.

Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known.

Teresa Mahoney, Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura and Samantha Swindler/The Oregonian For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population.

title_en: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
excerpt_en: The post Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Walter White baptizes a Followers of Christ member in 1951. He led an Oregon City, Oregon, offshoot of the sect. Courtesy of the Phillips family It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said.
“They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon.

The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches.

White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.”

Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.”

White’s grave in the Followers’ cemetery outside of Oregon City Beth Nakamura/The Oregonian To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings.

The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho, focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences.

Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated.

White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t.

In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation.

Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl.

Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households.

White, second from left in the back (in suspenders), with Followers leaders in Oregon City in 1937. By 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Courtesy of the Phillips family White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other.

As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.)

title_en: Jimmy Kimmel on Hegseth’s press conference amid impeachment attempt: ‘doozy of a performance’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts discussed embattled defense secretary’s defense of himself amid Republican-led effort to oust him
body_en: Late-night hosts recapped Pete Hegseth ’s press conference amid impeachment articles and Stephen Miller’s first day as White House chief of staff.

Jimmy Kimmel Tuesday marked “another busy day of dumb stuff here in the United States”, said Jimmy Kimmel that evening, including defense secretary – or self-proclaimed “secretary of war” – Hegseth’s press conference after articles of impeachment were introduced by outgoing representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky.

It was “a doozy of a performance” by the defense secretary. “He did exactly what members of the Trumper-verse do when they find themselves in a situation like this,” said Kimmel. “He smeared on the ChapStick. He got down on his knees and kissed the royal ass.”
Related: Jon Stewart on Trump’s testy 60 Minutes interview: ‘Was that sass?’
As Hegseth put it at the podium on Tuesday: “We’ve never had a better commander-in-chief. Full stop. I get to watch him every day. He lives and breathes ‘America first’.
“Any day he’ll have me, I’ll be right here at this podium,” he added.

“Well in that case, I now pronounce you husband and wife,” Kimmel joked. “That may have been the most romantic speech I’ve ever heard given by a secretary of war. Look out, Melania! Pretty Pete’s gunnin’ for your spot!”

Later on Tuesday, Republicans in the House voted to postpone the impeachment vote on Hegseth, instead referring it to committee. “Which means somebody’s having a shot of impeach-flavored schnapps at the Pentagon tonight, if you know what I mean,” the host quipped.

Seth Meyers And on Late Night, Seth Meyers also opened with the articles of impeachment against Hegseth brought by Massie, who said on the House floor: “Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office.”
“Oh man, you know someone’s mad when they call you your full name,” said Meyers. “Even today, if my mom called me Seth Adam Meyers, I would go straight to my room.”

Donald Trump, meanwhile, spent the first half of the week questioning the results of the election on Truth Social. “Oh yeah, because there’s no way someone as qualified as Darline Graham could’ve lost,” Meyers deadpanned, referring to the defeated Republican Senate candidate in South Carolina. “She’s someone’s sister!”
Related: Seth Meyers on Republicans: ‘Furiously backpedalling away from Trump’
In his forthcoming memoir, Joe Biden details his meeting in the Oval Office with Trump after the 2024 election, and says that Trump told him they “would’ve been good friends” if “not for politics”.
“What? How would they even have met?” Meyers said. “You really think this guy would’ve been allowed on the Amtrak quiet car?”
In other news, Monday marked Stephen Miller’s first day as White House chief of staff, “which is bad news for America, great news for his understudy at Rocky Horror Picture Show”, Meyers quipped.
Miller has at least one fan in RFK Jr, the president’s health and human services secretary, who praised the promotion and called on Miller to “unleash the Kraken”.
“So, first of all, the expression is ‘ release the Kraken’,” Meyers corrected. “And secondly, you only want him to release the Kraken so you can catch it and grill it.”

The host then turned to news that Trump’s wife, Melania, will star in a two-part docuseries from Amazon Prime Video. “Perfect for anyone who wants to learn more about her,” Meyers joked next to a photo of her husband.

And Elon Musk announced last week that Tesla will wind down production of its controversial Cybertruck. “So now if you want to get one, you’ll have to drive all the way down to the divorce court parking lot,” said Meyers.

title_en: Tell us: did you have a momentous life experience during the solar eclipse?
excerpt_en: We would like to hear from people who had incredible experiences during the solar eclipse in August this year
body_en: In August this year, many people stopped to witness the breathtaking solar eclipse.
Some peered through colanders to see the rare celestial event or joined friends and family to enjoy this special moment.

For others, it was a backdrop to a momentous life event. Perhaps you got engaged, married or even gave birth during the eclipse? Or maybe you had an extraordinary encounter with nature or enjoyed a memorable random act of kindness.
We’d like to hear your stories of extraordinary experiences during the solar eclipse. We would also love to see your pictures of these momentous moments.
